headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Endometritis
headings.content: Endometritis is defined as an inflammation or infection of the endometrium, which is the inner mucous membrane lining of the uterus. In clinical nursing practice, this condition is most frequently encountered in the postpartum period, known as postpartum endometritis, following vaginal delivery or cesarean section. However, it can also occur outside of pregnancy as pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) or as a result of intrauterine procedures like the insertion of an intrauterine device (IUD) or endometrial biopsy. As nursing students preparing for clinical practice and board examinations in Nigeria, recognizing the urgency of this condition is vital. Postpartum endometritis remains a significant cause of maternal morbidity and mortality if left untreated, making early detection and intervention critical components of postpartum nursing care. The condition typically manifests as localized uterine infection, but it possesses the potential to spread rapidly to the myometrium, parametrium, and general systemic circulation, leading to severe complications such as pelvic cellulitis, peritonitis, and septic shock. Understanding the baseline definition ensures that nurses can differentiate normal postpartum uterine involution, known as lochia, from pathological infectious processes that require immediate medical intervention and targeted antibiotic therapy.

headings.title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Endometrium
headings.content: A thorough understanding of the anatomy and physiology of the endometrium provides the foundational knowledge necessary for nursing students studying reproductive health. The endometrium is the innermost layer of the uterine wall, highly vascularized and responsive to cyclical fluctuations in ovarian hormones, namely estrogen and progesterone. It consists of two primary zones: the stratum functionalis and the stratum basale. The stratum functionalis is the superficial layer that undergoes thick proliferation, secretory changes, and subsequent shedding during menstruation if pregnancy does not occur. The stratum basale is the permanent, deeper layer that remains intact and supplies the regenerative stem cells needed to rebuild the functional layer during each cycle. Physiologically, the endometrium acts as the vital site of implantation for a fertilized ovum and supports early embryonic development through its rich glandular secretions and spiral arteries. During pregnancy, the endometrium undergoes extensive transformation into the decidua. Following childbirth, the site where the placenta was implanted undergoes a complex physiological healing process characterized by sloughing of the decidual tissue, thrombosis of open maternal blood vessels, and regeneration. When pathogens breach the protective cervical barrier during this vulnerable postpartum period, the normal physiological repair mechanism is disrupted, paving the way for localized infection, inflammation, impaired involution, and localized or systemic morbidity.

headings.title: Etiology and Risk Factors
headings.content: Etiology and risk factors for endometritis are diverse, encompassing both obstetric and non-obstetric origins. The etiology is typically polymicrobial, involving a combination of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria that ascend from the lower genital tract. Common causative organisms include Group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, and anaerobes like Bacteroides species, as well as sexually transmitted pathogens such as Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in non-obstetric cases. In the context of obstetric practice, the single greatest risk factor for developing postpartum endometritis is a cesarean delivery, particularly when performed after the rupture of membranes or during active labor. Other significant obstetric risk factors include prolonged rupture of membranes (PROM) lasting more than 18 to 24 hours, multiple digital vaginal examinations during labor, internal fetal monitoring, prolonged labor, manual removal of the placenta, postpartum hemorrhage, and lower socioeconomic status or poor nutritional status which compromises immune response. Non-obstetric risk factors include frequent or unprotected sexual intercourse, pelvic inflammatory disease, instrumentation of the uterus such as dilation and curettage (D&C), and IUD placement. Student nurses must systematically assess patients for these predisposing factors during admission and postpartum check-ups to implement appropriate preventive measures, such as sterile technique and prophylactic antibiotics.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Classification (Acute vs. Chronic)
headings.content: The pathophysiology of endometritis begins when endogenous or exogenous pathogens breach the normal protective barriers of the cervix and ascend into the uterine cavity. In the postpartum state, the large placental attachment site serves as an ideal, highly vascular, and nutrient-rich medium for bacterial proliferation. Once bacteria colonize the endometrial tissue, an inflammatory immune response is triggered, characterized by local vasodilation, leukocyte infiltration, edema, and tissue necrosis. Endometritis is clinically and pathologically classified into two main forms: acute and chronic. Acute endometritis is characterized by a heavy neutrophilic infiltration of the endometrial stroma, often resulting from bacterial infections following childbirth, miscarriage, or surgical procedures. If left untreated, acute infection can lead to abscess formation or systemic bacteremia. Chronic endometritis, on the other hand, is defined histologically by the presence of plasma cells within the endometrial stroma, alongside lymphocytes. Chronic forms are less acutely toxic and are frequently associated with retained products of conception, persistent low-grade infections (such as Chlamydia or tuberculosis), chronic IUD use, or submucosal leiomyomas. Chronic endometritis often presents with subtle symptoms like abnormal uterine bleeding or infertility, requiring careful histological examination for definitive diagnosis. Nursing students must appreciate this distinction, as management strategies and clinical presentations vary significantly between the acute and chronic disease states.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Symptoms
headings.content: Recognizing the clinical manifestations and symptoms of endometritis is a core competency for obstetric and medical-surgical nurses. In acute postpartum endometritis, symptoms typically manifest within the first few days following delivery, commonly between postpartum days two and five. The hallmark clinical sign is fever, often accompanied by tachycardia, chills, and lower abdominal or pelvic pain. Patients frequently present with uterine tenderness upon palpation during fundal checks. Another critical manifestation is abnormal, foul-smelling, or purulent lochia; although lochia can have a normal fleshy odor, a distinctly foul or putrid smell strongly indicates bacterial infection and tissue necrosis. Subinvolution of the uterus, where the uterus remains large, boggy, and fails to return to its normal non-pregnant size, is another classic physical finding during nursing assessment. Patients may also report general malaise, fatigue, and headache. In contrast, chronic endometritis presents with a much milder clinical picture. Symptoms of chronic endometritis often include abnormal uterine bleeding, such as intermenstrual spotting or menorrhagia, lower abdominal discomfort, dyspareunia, and unexplained infertility or recurrent pregnancy losses. Nursing students must remain vigilant during routine postpartum assessments, as missing early signs of acute infection can lead to rapid clinical deterioration. Documenting the character, amount, and odor of lochia alongside vital sign trends is vital for early detection.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Nursing Assessment
headings.content: Diagnostic evaluation and comprehensive nursing assessment play an essential role in confirming endometritis and guiding treatment. When a nurse suspects endometritis based on clinical findings such as fever, uterine tenderness, and foul lochia, immediate reporting to the attending physician is required. The diagnostic process begins with a thorough physical and pelvic examination, noting fundal height, consistency, and tenderness. Vital signs must be monitored closely for signs of systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) or sepsis. Laboratory investigations are crucial: a complete blood count (CBC) typically reveals leukocytosis with a left shift, indicating an active bacterial infection. Urinalysis and urine culture are ordered to rule out urinary tract infections, which present similarly. Endometrial or lochial cultures can be collected using sterile technique, though blood cultures are indicated if the patient experiences high spiking fevers or rigors to check for bacteremia. Imaging studies, such as a pelvic ultrasound, are invaluable to evaluate the uterine cavity for retained products of conception (RPOC) or abnormal fluid collections. In cases of chronic endometritis where symptoms are subtle, an endometrial biopsy processed for histological examination is the gold standard diagnostic tool. Nurses must prepare the patient emotionally and physically for these diagnostic procedures, explain each step, ensure comfort, and accurately record all test results in the patient's chart.

headings.title: Medical and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Medical and pharmacological management of endometritis focuses on eradicating the infectious agents, controlling inflammation, and preventing severe systemic complications. The cornerstone of treatment for acute postpartum endometritis is broad-spectrum intravenous (IV) antibiotic therapy. Because the infection is typically polymicrobial, combination regimens are standard practice. The classic first-line regimen includes clindamycin combined with an aminoglycoside (such as gentamicin), which provides excellent coverage against both aerobic and anaerobic bacteria. Alternative regimens may include broad-spectrum beta-lactams or cephalosporins. Antibiotic therapy is usually continued intravenously until the patient has been afebrile and clinically asymptomatic for at least 24 to 48 hours; oral antibiotics are rarely required following a successful IV course unless specific pathogens dictate otherwise. In addition to antimicrobials, supportive care is vital. This includes adequate intravenous hydration, pain management using analgesics or antipyretics, and monitoring fluid balance. If diagnostic evaluations reveal retained products of conception as the underlying etiology or a contributing factor to the infection, surgical management in the form of dilation and curettage (D&C) or gentle uterine evacuation is performed under appropriate antibiotic cover. Nurses play a critical role in administering prescribed antibiotics on strict schedules, monitoring for adverse drug reactions, and evaluating the patient's therapeutic response.

headings.title: Nursing Care Plan and Patient Education
headings.content: A comprehensive nursing care plan for a patient with endometritis requires meticulous assessment, targeted nursing diagnoses, and thorough patient education. Priority nursing diagnoses often include Risk for Fluid Volume Deficit related to fever and infection, Acute Pain related to uterine inflammation and involution, and Deficient Knowledge regarding the condition and self-care management. Nursing interventions include monitoring vital signs every four hours, assessing lochia amount, color, and odor, performing fundal assessments with gentle palpation, and administering prescribed intravenous antibiotics and analgesics precisely on schedule. Encouraging early ambulation and deep breathing exercises helps prevent venous stasis and pulmonary complications. Patient education is a paramount responsibility for nursing students to master. Nurses must educate the patient and her family on the importance of completing the entire prescribed course of medications, recognizing warning signs of worsening infection (such as persistent high fever, severe abdominal pain, or heavy bleeding), and practicing good perineal hygiene, including proper handwashing and changing sanitary pads frequently. For breastfeeding mothers receiving antibiotics, the nurse must provide guidance regarding medication safety during lactation. Finally, scheduling and emphasizing the importance of a postpartum follow-up visit ensures complete clinical recovery and emotional well-being.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Prognosis
headings.content: While most cases of endometritis resolve successfully with prompt antibiotic therapy, failing to recognize and treat the condition can lead to severe potential complications and a guarded prognosis. As nursing students, understanding these risks highlights the importance of vigilant clinical monitoring. Potential complications of untreated or inadequately treated endometritis include pelvic cellulitis (spread of infection into the parametrium), generalized peritonitis, and intra-pelvic abscess formation. Furthermore, severe infection can precipitate septic thrombophlebitis, where infected blood clots form in the pelvic veins and pose a high risk of pulmonary embolism. Systemic spread can lead to sepsis and septic shock, which are life-threatening medical emergencies requiring intensive care unit admission. In chronic or recurrent cases, long-term complications involve chronic pelvic pain, intrauterine adhesions (known as Asherman's syndrome), tubal factor infertility, and an increased risk of ectopic pregnancy in future conceptions due to anatomical distortion of the reproductive tract. The overall prognosis for acute postpartum endometritis is generally excellent when diagnosed early and managed with appropriate broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy. However, delayed intervention drastically increases morbidity, hospital stay lengths, and the risk of permanent reproductive impairment. Nurses serve as the frontline defense in intercepting these complications through timely assessment, patient advocacy, and rigorous adherence to infection control protocols.
